table.veg_type: Sedge/graminoid fen (Carex, Calamagrostis; natural minerotrophic fen)
table.basis: Share of vascular NPP. In the field, NPP here is peak aboveground biomass plus root production from ingrowth bags. Measured values in undisturbed fen: Carex rostrata 0.38 and Calamagrostis canadensis 0.28 (Graf 2009). Values that sit near the typical: the modelling convention BNPP = 0.5 ANPP, which gives 0.33 (Campbell 2000 and Thormann 2001, cited by Graf 2009), and the PVN prior for sedges of 0.30 (RS 0.7). The upper end, 0.80, comes from two sources: the Reader & Stewart 1972 peatland range of 0.28-0.80 (secondary, cited by Graf 2009) and the HPM minerotrophic sedge AGfrac of 0.2, which gives 0.80 belowground (a model parameter adapted from Bauer 2004; Frolking 2010). Two colonizers of a drier, restored fen gave 0.08 (Scirpus cyperinus) and 0.14 (Juncus), and are excluded from the natural-fen range. Biomass is not NPP: the Mer Bleue fen fine-root share of biomass is 0.86 (above to fine-below ratio 0.16:1; Moore 2002), and the LPJ-WHy flood-tolerant graminoid leaf:root target of 0.4 gives 0.71 root biomass (Wania 2009). Exudates: 0.06 of NPP is the PVN sedge prior (REX 0.2 x 0.3, with the spring factor set to 1). It is included within the 0.30 belowground share. It is a model value, not a measurement. Ingrowth bags probably under-catch rhizome production.

table.veg_type: Sphagnum bog, whole ecosystem (open ombrotrophic bog: ericoid shrubs + Sphagnum + minor sedges)
table.basis: Share of annual litter input to the peat, taken as NPP because the paper assumes NPP equals litter fall; the total is about 300 g C m-2 yr-1 at Mer Bleue. Roots are 161-176 g C m-2 yr-1, giving 0.54-0.59 of 300 or 0.53-0.58 of the 305 sum of components. The roots were not measured: they are the residual left after moss litter (54), vascular leaf litter (about 45) and shoots overgrown by moss (30-45) are subtracted from the assumed total, so the root share is circular. There is only one whole-ecosystem estimate for an open bog. Fine-root biomass (not NPP) at the bog hummocks and hollows is 1:1 with aboveground biomass, a share of 0.5, and this leaves out coarse roots (Moore 2002).

table.veg_type: Sphagnum bog, Sphagnum / brown moss component
table.basis: Structural: mosses have no roots, and every model puts moss NPP into the surface litter cohort. HPM uses AGfrac 1.0 for all moss PFTs (Frolking 2010), and PVN uses RS 1.0 with REX 0.0 for Sphagnum and brown moss (Lippmann 2023). ELM-SPRUCE is the one exception: it gives Sphagnum a fine-root pool (froot_leaf 0.3944) as a stand-in for non-photosynthetic tissue (Shi 2021). The moss share of ecosystem NPP varies a lot between sites: 0.53 at SPRUCE S1 (Sphagnum 208 of 395 g C m-2 yr-1; Hanson 2020) and about 0.12-0.18 at Mer Bleue (moss 35-54 of about 300; Moore 2002).

Share of shrub NPP, with fine and coarse roots together only in the models. ELM-SPRUCE optimized allocation gives 0.42; I derived this from froot_leaf 0.6862, stem_leaf 0.754 and croot_stem 0.754 (Shi 2021), and the paper does not state the fraction. HPM uses 0.50 for ombrotrophic shrubs (AGfrac 0.5; Frolking 2010). Field minirhizotron data at SPRUCE S1, counting absorptive fine roots only, give 0.27 in 2011 and 0.06 in 2012; the authors prefer 2012 because 2011 is inflated by roots colonizing the new tubes (Iversen 2018). Moore 2002 gives a residual root share of about 0.66-0.72 of vascular NPP (roots 161-176 of about 245), which includes the minor sedges. I set the typical at 0.42, the median of the point estimates.

Root production as a share of total annual vascular NPP, with mosses excluded. A pan-Arctic synthesis of five studies gives a range of 30-90% in sedge-dominated tundra (Iversen 2015). The typical value 0.6 is the midpoint of that range, not a central estimate published by the authors. For Eriophorum vaginatum at tussock scale, Chapin 1988 (cited by Sullivan 2005) gives 0.75 of total production in water tracks and 0.90 outside them. Biomass is not NPP: the median belowground:aboveground ratio for sedges is 5.1, a share of 0.84 that includes rhizomes and storage organs (Iversen 2015). For contrast, shrub-dominated tundra gives 10-60% (Iversen 2015). The source says 'sedge-dominated tundra' and does not specifically mean wet sedge meadows.

table.veg_type: Emergent marsh, freshwater inland (Typha latifolia; Cyperus papyrus)
table.basis: Share of annual production from harvests, with crown bases counted as belowground. San Joaquin Typha marsh, 1999-2007: BNPP/(ANPP+BNPP) = 308/1023 = 0.30, with annual values of 0.24-0.37 (derived from Table 2). Measured belowground shares are 0.29 for 2006 and 0.46 for 2007, of which crown bases are 22-33%, roots 2-4% and rhizomes 3-11%. After the paper's starch-reserve correction, BNPP/NPP is 0.36 (Rocha 2009). For papyrus at Lake Naivasha, belowground is the difference between modelled total NPP (6.28 kg dw m-2 yr-1) and measured shoot NPP (5150), giving 0.18 (derived; Jones 1997). The papyrus rhizome+root:shoot biomass ratio is 1.38:1, and the stock is mostly rhizome (4426 vs 90 g m-2 of roots). The PVN Typha prior is 0.30 (Lippmann 2023). Exudates: 0.06 of NPP is the PVN Typha prior (REX 0.2), a model value only.

table.veg_type: Emergent marsh, Phragmites australis reed beds (tidal / brackish)
table.basis: The bases are mixed. Westlake 1982 (cited by Soetaert 2004) gives an above:below production ratio of 0.34-1.4, which is a belowground share of 0.42-0.75. Smalley-method NAPP compiled by Stagg 2016 gives 0.72 for the Po Delta (Scarton 2002) and 0.58-0.74 for Delaware (Roman & Daiber 1984); the Delaware bounds combine unpaired ranges. A calibrated growth model for the Scheldt estuary gives 0.45 of assimilates flowing belowground at the oligohaline site and 0.54 at the mesohaline site. Those model figures are gross allocation and include root and rhizome maintenance respiration, so they are not NPP (Soetaert 2004). Peak biomass there is more than 60% belowground. I set the typical at about 0.6, the median of the point estimates.

table.veg_type: Emergent marsh, coastal Gulf / estuarine (Panicum-Typha fresh, Sagittaria-Schoenoplectus intermediate, Spartina patens brackish)
table.basis: Share of above plus belowground net annual primary production (NAPP), measured with the Smalley method on serial cores that reached only 30 cm. Values for coastal Louisiana: fresh 3883/4930 = 0.79, intermediate 4679/5735 = 0.82, and brackish 5609/7096 = 0.79 (Stagg 2016). Belowground exceeded aboveground in every wetland type. The low end is St Lawrence Scirpus americanus at 0.64 (Giroux & Bedard 1988, compiled by Stagg 2016); its units look inconsistent, but the ratio holds if both values share a unit. The same genus Typha scores 0.79 here with Smalley coring and 0.30 in California from harvests (Rocha 2009). The method explains more of the difference than the vegetation does.

table.veg_type: Tropical peat swamp forest, hardwood / mixed (SE Asia, Micronesia, pan-tropical)
table.basis: Fine-root production as a share of NPP or of carbon inputs to the peat. Coarse roots are almost never measured. Values: 0.17 of plant productivity, or 17-23% of carbon inputs (Hergoualc'h & Verchot 2011, cited by Dezzeo 2021); 0.155 in HPMTrop's monthly litter inputs, a model parameter set from the same literature (Kurnianto 2015); 0.10 in Kosrae (Chimner 2005); 0.095 in a synthesis of 7 peat studies (Sjogersten 2014). Riau, Sumatra gives fine roots at 0-20 cm divided by (litterfall + fine roots) of 0.174 on mounds, 0.141 on non-mound floors and 0.068 in gaps (Shimamura 2005). Coarse roots are either 'considered minimal' (Chimner & Ewel 2005, cited by Dezzeo 2021) or about 0.07, a figure taken from upland forest (Malhi 2011, cited by Sjogersten 2014). Total belowground is therefore about 0.15-0.25. All the root data come from the top 20-25 cm.

table.veg_type: Tropical peat swamp forest, palm-dominated (Mauritia flexuosa, Raphia)
table.basis: Share of detrital carbon input to the peat: fine-root mortality 3.4 +/- 1.3 divided by (litterfall 4.9 + root mortality), in Mg C ha-1 yr-1, at an intact Mauritia swamp in Peru. This gives 0.41 (derived). The range 0.30-0.49 is my derivation from +/- 1 SE of root mortality. Fine roots were sampled to 25 cm only and coarse roots are excluded (Hergoualc'h 2023). Fine-root productivity at the same site is 3.7 +/- 1.2 (Dezzeo 2021). In the Congo, palm-swamp fine-root production of 2.6 +/- 0.3 exceeds the hardwood swamp (1.9) and terra firme (1.7), but the study measured no aboveground NPP, so it gives no fraction (Sciumbata 2023). The estimate rests on a single site.

table.veg_type: Boreal treed peatland, vascular plants (Picea mariana / Larix bog, black spruce and alder peatland)
table.basis: Mixed partial bases, no study measures both fine and coarse roots. The typical 0.25 is my estimate, not a published figure. It adds the SPRUCE vascular fine-root share of 0.17 (BNPP 32 of vascular NPP 187; Hanson 2020) and a coarse-root share of about 0.07 from the same Marcell Experimental Forest (black spruce 0.068 and alder 0.08, coarse roots from allometry, fine roots excluded; Weishampel 2009). This sum over-simplifies because the two denominators differ. Other values: the tree fine-root share of tree NPP at SPRUCE is 0.45 in 2012 (the preferred year) and 0.70 in 2011; for shrubs it is 0.06 and 0.27 (Iversen 2018). The Alberta treed bog gives 0.154 for trees only, set by an allometric root:shoot ratio of 0.222 (Munir 2015). At the same SPRUCE site, the minirhizotron method gives a fine-root share of 0.45 and ingrowth cores give 0.17.

table.veg_type: Boreal treed peatland, whole ecosystem including Sphagnum
table.basis: Share of total ecosystem NPP, with Sphagnum included. At SPRUCE S1 before treatment, fine-root BNPP to 30 cm is 32 of 395 g C m-2 yr-1, or 0.081; its SD (39) exceeds the mean. At the same site Sphagnum is 0.527 and vascular aboveground 0.392 (Hanson 2020). For a Marcell black spruce subplot, whose ANPP includes Sphagnum, coarse roots alone are 0.068 (Weishampel 2009). The typical 0.15 is my derived sum of the fine-root and coarse-root terms from different plots. Both components are lower bounds.

table.veg_type: Floodplain / riverine forested wetland (temperate swamp forest, tidal varzea)
table.basis: No verified row pairs aboveground and belowground NPP, so no fraction can be computed. What exists: Great Dismal Swamp root production of 59-989 g m-2 yr-1 across four stands (Powell 1991); coastal North Carolina fine-root production of 455 g m-2 yr-1 at 0-20 cm (Li 2019); and varzea litterfall of 13.8 Mg ha-1 yr-1 plus a root biomass stock of 35.6 Mg ha-1 (Cattanio 2004). All the qualitative evidence points one way: more flooding means less production allocated belowground (Day 1993; Powell 1991; bald cypress saplings, Megonigal 1992). This implies a share below the upland tropical fine-root reference of 0.27 (Malhi 2011), but that is an inference. Mangroves are described only as 'nearly identical' in allocation to other tropical forests (Alongi 2014).

Fine-root share of measured NPP across 35 sites: 27 +/- 11%, with canopy at 34% and wood at 39%. Coarse and other belowground wood sits inside the wood term, added as 21 +/- 4% of woody production; this is about 0.07 of NPP as cited by Sjogersten 2014. The range is +/- 1 SD. The exudate and mycorrhizal share of 'about 10 per cent of NPP' is a hedged estimate that uses mycorrhizal respiration as a proxy. The paper's own sensitivity test uses 50% of fine-root NPP, about 0.12-0.14 (Malhi 2011). No sites in the dataset are wetlands.

table.veg_type: Root exudates, all vascular wetland types (model priors only)
table.basis: In this row the range is the exudate share of NPP, not the belowground share. No verified row measures wetland exudation in the field. LPJ-WHyMe: fexu 0.175 in Table 1, but 0.15 is the calibrated 'final' value in the same paper, with site-best values of 0.10-0.15 and a tested range of 0.05-0.20. It applies to total NPP and is not specific to any PFT. The pool turns over at kexu 13 a-1 at 10 C. The authors justify it with 15-20% of photosynthesized carbon, which is not NPP (Wania 2010; Wania 2009). PVN: sedges and Typha 0.06, tall grass 0.03, short grass 0.011, taken out of root production and boosted in spring by KSP 0.4/0.2/0.1 (Lippmann 2023). The size of the spring factor is not given. The upland tropical proxy is about 0.10 (Malhi 2011). The models disagree by a factor of 2.5-15, and the two model families account for exudates differently.

notes: Share of aboveground litter that ends below the water table: no verified row measures this for any vegetation type (sweep row 46 found nothing). Everything below is inference from verified pieces. (1) Bogs and treed peatlands, where the water table is below the surface (Mer Bleue: -25 cm in the fen, -30 to -50 cm in the bog). Leaf and moss litter lands on oxic peat, and HPM and HPMTrop put all aboveground NPP into the surface cohort (Frolking 2010; Kurnianto 2015). On an annual scale the share below the water table is close to 0. It rises only through burial or a rising water table. The one quantified burial route is shrub shoots overgrown by moss: 30-45 g C m-2 yr-1, which is 0.10-0.15 of total litter input (my calculation, 30/305 to 45/305; Moore 2002). (2) Hummock-hollow swamp forests. At Alligator River, hollows are 40% of the area and are under water more than 70% of the year (Li 2019). If litter fell evenly across space and time, about 0.4 x 0.7 = 0.28 of litterfall would land in standing water. That is my estimate. (3) Swamps and floodplains that are inundated most of the time. In the Congo peat swamps the water table sits at or above the surface most of the year (Sciumbata 2023). Non-mound floors in Riau flood often; the water table reaches +18.7 cm against a mean of -30.3 cm (Shimamura 2005). In black-water igapo the leaf-fall pulse comes at peak flood (Adis 1979, cited by Cattanio 2004). In such systems a majority of aboveground litter plausibly lands in water or saturated peat. (4) Marshes. Typha crown bases are 22-33% of annual production and are counted as belowground (Rocha 2009); they sit at the sediment-water interface. Whether a model books them as aboveground or belowground changes the anoxic input by about 0.2-0.3 of NPP. Overall plausible range: about 0 in hummock bogs, about 0.1-0.15 through moss burial in bogs, about 0.3 in hummock-hollow swamps, and more than 0.5 in permanently flooded swamps and marshes.

Root placement relative to the water table matters for methanogens more than the total belowground share does. Sedges put roots at or below the water table: at the Mer Bleue fen, sedge root biomass peaks at 30-50 cm with the water table at -25 cm, and small amounts reach 1 m (Moore 2002). Bog shrubs and trees keep their live fine roots above it. Shrub roots do not go below the growing-season water table (Moore 2002). New fine roots at SPRUCE grow in aerobic peat above the water table, and the roots below the maximum summer water table are dead and 4000-6000 years old (Iversen 2018). On wet sites, spruce and tamarack roots are confined to hummocks (Lieffers 1987). So in bogs and treed peatlands, root litter and exudates mostly feed oxic decomposition. In fens, wet tundra and marshes they enter anoxic peat directly. The models encode this differently. HPM puts 80% of sedge root litter in the top 0.3 m and spreads other vascular roots evenly down to max(water table, 0.2 m) (Frolking 2010). LPJ-WHyMe puts about 60% of graminoid root biomass in a fixed 0.3 m acrotelm and 40% below it (Wania 2010). HPMTrop roots reach down to max(0.5 m, water table) (Kurnianto 2015). In the Congo, 68-92% of fine-root production lies in the top 30 cm, where the peat is saturated most of the year (Sciumbata 2023). At Alligator River, 23% of fine-root production is in hollows that are under water more than 70% of the year; this is a proxy and the paper does not state the number (Li 2019).

Substrate quality and turnover. HPM initial decay rates put sedge litter (k0 0.57 minerotrophic, 0.32 ombrotrophic) 2.5-10 times above Sphagnum (0.06-0.13) (Frolking 2010). So a sedge-dominated fen gives methanogens both deeper root inputs and faster-decaying inputs. In Neotropical peat, roots decompose up to 5 times faster at the surface than at 50 cm, and the peat is built mostly of roots and stems (Hoyos-Santillan 2015). Deep root litter therefore persists and becomes a slow substrate. Fresh exudates near the root tips are the fast pool; LPJ-WHyMe turns exudates over at 13 a-1 at 10 C, which is roughly monthly (Wania 2010). Wetter conditions lower belowground allocation (Day 1993; Megonigal 1992; Powell 1991), but they also make a larger share of the root input anoxic. The two effects work against each other in a model.

The measurement basis and method move the numbers more than vegetation type does. For the same genus, Typha scores 0.79 with Smalley serial coring (Stagg 2016) and 0.30 with harvests plus crown-base BNPP (Rocha 2009). At the same SPRUCE bog, tree fine roots measured by minirhizotron give 0.45-0.70 (Iversen 2018), while vascular fine roots from ingrowth cores give 0.17 (Hanson 2020). Biomass ratios should not stand in for NPP shares: Mer Bleue fen gives 0.86, tundra sedges 0.84 and papyrus 0.58 belowground by biomass. Standing belowground stocks, mostly rhizomes, turn over more slowly than leaves. The denominators also differ across rows: total NPP (Graf, Iversen, Rocha, Malhi); litter or carbon input to the peat (Moore, Kurnianto, Dezzeo, Hergoualc'h); litterfall plus fine roots (Shimamura); gross assimilate allocation that includes root respiration (Soetaert); and Smalley NAPP to 30 cm (Stagg). Most field fractions count fine roots only and are lower bounds.

Pattern useful for parameterizing a model that splits root litter from leaf litter. Graminoid-dominated types (wet tundra 0.3-0.9, coastal marsh 0.64-0.82 by Smalley, sedge fen 0.28-0.8) send more to belowground than woody wetland types (tropical hardwood peat swamp about 0.15-0.25, boreal treed peatland about 0.07-0.45 vascular, bog shrubs 0.06-0.72 with a model value of about 0.42). Mosses contribute 0 by construction. Freshwater Typha and papyrus measured by harvest or difference (0.18-0.46) sit closer to the woody group than to the Smalley-based coastal marshes. The main difference between these two groups is where the roots sit relative to the water table (see the root-placement note).

Which numbers I derived. These are my own arithmetic on verified source numbers, not values the papers print: Moore 2002 shares 0.53-0.59 and 0.66-0.72 of vascular NPP, and 0.10-0.15 for moss burial; Shi 2021 shrub share 0.42; Jones 1997 0.18; Rocha 2009 0.30 multi-year; all Stagg 2016 ratios; Shimamura 2005 ratios; Hergoualc'h 2023 0.41 and its +/- SE range 0.30-0.49; Hanson 2020 shares; Weishampel 2009 shares; Sjogersten 2014 0.095; the boreal sums 0.25 and 0.15; and the Li 2019 hollow share 0.23. These are secondary citations: Reader & Stewart 1972, Campbell 2000, Thormann 2001 (via Graf 2009); Chapin 1988 (via Sullivan 2005); Westlake 1982 (via Soetaert 2004); Scarton 2002, Roman & Daiber 1984 and Giroux & Bedard 1988 (via Stagg 2016); Hergoualc'h & Verchot 2011 (via Dezzeo 2021 and Kurnianto 2015). The bibliographic fields for the sources listed come from the Crossref records attached to the rows. Before this goes into a formal document, re-query each DOI against Crossref.
gaps: No verified field measurement of the share of aboveground litter, or of NPP, that enters soil below the water table, for any vegetation type. All the statements are qualitative or from models.

No field measurement of root exudation in any wetland. Every exudate fraction (0.011-0.175 of NPP) is a model prior. LPJ-WHyMe disagrees with itself (Table 1 gives 0.175, the calibrated value is 0.15), and the size of the PVN spring factor f(KSP) is not reported.

Floodplain and riverine forest has no paired aboveground and belowground NPP, so no fraction exists. There is only root production (Powell 1991; Li 2019), a root stock (Cattanio 2004) and qualitative statements about flooding. Mangroves have only a qualitative statement (Alongi 2014).

Tropical peat swamp forests: coarse roots are never measured (none of the 7 studies in Sjogersten 2014). Fine roots are sampled only to 20-25 cm. The Congo study has no aboveground NPP. Palm swamps rest on one site (Hergoualc'h 2023). The primary review Hergoualc'h & Verchot 2011 was not accessed, and the Chimner 2005 full text is paywalled.
Open Sphagnum bog has one whole-ecosystem estimate (Moore 2002), in which the root term is a residual and not a measurement.
Sedge fen has one field study (Graf 2009, ingrowth bags, 2 natural-fen species) that probably misses rhizome production. The HPM sedge value of 0.8 traces to Bauer 2004, which was not checked.
Wet tundra has only a pooled 30-90% range and tussock-scale values from secondary citations (Chapin 1988). There is no ecosystem-scale NPP partition specific to wet sedge meadows.

Boreal treed peatland: no study measures fine and coarse roots together, and the shrub and herb belowground NPP is missing at Marcell (Weishampel 2009). At SPRUCE the two methods give fine-root shares that differ by a factor of 2.6.

Papyrus: 0.18 comes from dry-weight numbers against a modelled total NPP. One check note says the paper's Fig. 3, in carbon units, contradicts this split, and that fraction check was not among the verified rows. Treat 0.18 as unconfirmed.
PVN site-calibrated RS and REX (Lippmann 2023 Tables S6/S7) were not seen. Only the Table 1 priors are used.

Rhizome turnover, meaning how much of the belowground production dies each year and becomes substrate, is not quantified for any type. Belowground stocks in papyrus, tundra sedges and Phragmites are dominated by rhizomes.

Moore 2002 (J Ecol 90:25-36, 2002_Moore.txt ~l.236-258, 435-441) reports root biomass only, not NPP. It says bog shrub fine roots do not extend beneath the growing-season WT (about -50 cm at the hummock, -30 cm in the hollow). At the fen, sedge root biomass peaked at 30-50 cm, just below the WT (-25 cm), and small amounts (10-20 g m-2) reached 1 m. The text gives no fraction below WT, though one could be read off the Fig. 2 biomass profiles.

Wallen 1987 (Holarctic Ecol 10:73-79, l.310-322) is qualitative only. Hummock living roots reach down to the WT; in lower plots, belowground biomass reaches about 15 cm below the WT. Wallen 1986 does not mention the WT.

Iversen 2018 (iversen2018.txt l.11-15, 372-384, 464-471) is qualitative on the WT. Fine-root growth is shallow and above the growing-season WT; the fine roots below the maximum summer WT are dead and 4000-6000 yr old. Its numbers are different quantities: depth coefficients for fine-root production (beta 0.726-0.886) and the fine-root share of whole-plant NPP (16-85% for trees, 1-47% for shrubs). Neither is a below-WT fraction.

Frolking 2010 HPM (l.380-386) uses a model profile, following Bauer 2004. 80% of sedge root litter goes into the top 0.3 m, and other vascular plants have a constant profile down to max(annual WT, 0.2 m).

Wania 2010 (l.155-181) uses an exponential root-biomass profile (lambda 25.17 cm) fitted to field cores (Gallego-Sala 2008; Bernard & Fiala 1986). About 60% of root biomass sits in a fixed 0.3 m acrotelm. That is biomass relative to a fixed depth, not NPP relative to the WT.

Other alloc sources give no direct figure either. Murphy & Moore 2010 (abstract only) is qualitative: a deeper WT raises root production at depth. Munir 2015 cites 6% of root biomass below 20 cm in a drained bog. Congo 2023 gives 68-92% of fine-root production in the top 30 cm at forest sites where the WT is at or above the surface most of the year. That implies a below-WT share indirectly, but it is a forest site, not herb, and gives no stated fraction.
